questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates the economic problem of scarcity?
options: The Central Bank issues new N2000 notes to replace old ones
A trader in Lagos increases price of tomatoes after a weekend market festival
A family in Enugu saves part of their income for future school fees
A farmer in Kano has enough land to grow either maize or sorghum but not both, and must choose which to plant
questions.explanation: Scarcity arises when resources are limited relative to wants; the farmer must choose between maize and sorghum because the land cannot produce both. The trader raising prices is a response to demand; saving is choice over time but not scarcity per se; issuing notes is monetary policy, not an illustration of scarce resources.

questions.q: Which statement best describes opportunity cost?
options: The cost of producing one additional unit of a good
The total money spent on all alternatives when making a decision
The value of the next best alternative foregone when a choice is made
The benefit gained from the least preferred option among choices
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is specifically the value of the next best alternative not chosen. Total money spent is not opportunity cost; benefit from the least preferred option is irrelevant; cost of producing one more unit refers to marginal cost, not opportunity cost.

questions.q: If the government of Abuja sets a price ceiling below the market equilibrium for bread, the most likely immediate effect is:
options: No change in market because consumers will pay more elsewhere
Surplus of bread as quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Long-term increase in bread quality due to competition
Shortage of bread as quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
questions.explanation: A binding price ceiling below equilibrium increases quantity demanded and reduces quantity supplied, causing shortage. A surplus occurs with price floors. Consumers paying more elsewhere contradicts a binding low ceiling, and quality increasing is unlikely when suppliers face lower prices.

questions.q: A town in Ondo had 5,000 employed workers and 500 unemployed persons actively seeking work. What is the unemployment rate (to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: Labour force = employed + unemployed = 5,000 + 500 = 5,500. Unemployment rate = (500 / 5,500) × 100 = 9.0909...% ≈ 9.1%. 10.0% would be if unemployed were 556; 8.3% corresponds to 500/6,000; 5.0% is 500/10,000.

questions.q: Which policy would most directly reduce structural unemployment in Nigeria?
options: Providing vocational training to match workers' skills with available jobs
Printing more money to stimulate demand
Reducing the retirement age across public service
Raising the minimum wage for all sectors
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment stems from mismatches between skills and jobs; vocational training directly addresses this. Raising minimum wage may increase unemployment in some sectors, printing money targets demand not structural issues, and reducing retirement age affects labour supply but not skill mismatches.

questions.q: A factory fires 200 workers due to automation. Which type of unemployment is this most likely to cause?
options: Classical unemployment
Structural unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
questions.explanation: Automation changes the structure of demand for labour, causing structural unemployment as workers' skills become obsolete. Seasonal unemployment relates to time-bound jobs; frictional is short-term job search; classical unemployment arises from wages being above equilibrium.

questions.q: If Nigeria's nominal GDP in 2024 is N120 trillion and the GDP deflator index (base year 2020=100) is 150, what is real GDP in 2020 prices?
options: N120.0 trillion
N180.0 trillion
N80.0 trillion
N200.0 trillion
questions.explanation: Real GDP = Nominal GDP × (100 / GDP deflator) = 120 × (100/150) = 120 × 2/3 = 80 trillion naira. 180 would be multiplying by 1.5; 120 assumes deflator = 100; 200 has no relation to the formula.

questions.q: Which of the following is included in Nigeria's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) but not in Gross National Product (GNP)?
options: Income sent to Nigeria by Nigerians working abroad
Remittances received by a Nigerian family from a relative in the UK
Profits earned in Nigeria by a foreign-owned oil company
Income earned by Nigerian-owned firms operating in Ghana
questions.explanation: GDP counts production within the country regardless of ownership; profits of a foreign-owned oil company in Nigeria are included in GDP but not GNP. Income sent to Nigeria by Nigerians abroad and remittances are part of GNP (national income) but not necessarily GDP; income earned by Nigerian firms abroad counts in GNP, not GDP.

questions.q: A Lagos bakery has total fixed cost N30,000 per month. At output 1,000 loaves total cost is N70,000. What is average variable cost (AVC) per loaf at this output?
options: N70 per loaf
N40 per loaf
N100 per loaf
N30 per loaf
questions.explanation: Total variable cost = Total cost − Fixed cost = 70,000 − 30,000 = 40,000. AVC = 40,000 / 1,000 = N40 per loaf. N70 is TC/output (70,000/1,000), N30 is FC/output, and N100 is incorrect.

questions.q: If a firm faces price taker conditions and market price is N10 per unit, marginal cost (MC) equals N10 at output 500 but average total cost (ATC) at 500 units is N12. To maximise profit (or minimise loss), the firm should:
options: Reduce output to where ATC equals price
Produce 500 units in the short run if price covers average variable cost, because MC = MR = price
Immediately shut down since ATC > price
Produce more until ATC falls to N10
questions.explanation: In perfect competition MR = price = N10; profit maximisation occurs where MC = MR (MC = 10 at 500). Even if ATC > price (loss), the firm should continue if price covers AVC. Shutting down is wrong unless price < AVC. Producing more to lower ATC may not equate MC=MR; reducing output to where ATC = price ignores MC condition.

questions.q: Olufunke runs a small hair-salon in Ibadan where many similar salons offer nearly identical services and customers can easily switch between them. Which market structure best describes her industry?
options: Monopoly
Monopolistic competition
Oligopoly
Perfect competition
questions.explanation: Many firms offering similar but differentiated services with free entry is monopolistic competition. It is not perfect competition because salons differentiate through location and style; not oligopoly because there are many firms; not monopoly because no single salon controls the market.

questions.q: A cement firm in Enugu has patent protection allowing it to be sole producer of a new low-cost cement for several years. Which feature is most characteristic of the firm's market during the patent period?
options: Price maker with restricted entry for rival firms
Numerous close substitutes exist so firm is a price taker
Firms collude to set output and share market
Free entry and exit guarantee normal profits only
questions.explanation: A patent grants temporary monopoly power, making the firm a price maker and restricting entry. It is not a price taker because substitutes are limited; free entry does not apply; collusion is irrelevant for a single patented firm.

questions.q: In an industry with only three large firms that often match each other's prices and outputs, which strategy best explains their behaviour?
options: Interdependence leading to strategic behaviour (as in an oligopoly)
Monopolistic pricing by a single dominant firm
Non-price competition cannot occur in such an industry
Independent price taking as in perfect competition
questions.explanation: Few large firms cause interdependence and strategic behaviour typical of oligopoly. They are not independent price takers; non-price competition can and often does occur; there is no single dominant monopolist in a symmetric three-firm oligopoly.

questions.q: The Federal Government of Nigeria increases value-added tax (VAT). Which immediate effect is most likely?
options: No effect on revenue but increase in investment
Decrease in government revenue and lower consumer prices
Increase in money supply causing inflation
Increase in government revenue and higher prices for consumers
questions.explanation: Raising VAT raises government revenue and typically raises consumer prices (tax incidence). It does not decrease revenue or lower prices; it does not directly increase investment; it is not a monetary action that changes money supply.

questions.q: Nigeria issues long-term government bonds and uses proceeds to build highways. This action is best described as:
options: Contractionary monetary policy
A current expenditure financed by taxes
Reducing public debt through privatization
Financing a capital expenditure by borrowing
questions.explanation: Issuing bonds to build highways is borrowing to finance capital expenditure. It does not reduce public debt; it is fiscal borrowing, not monetary policy; it is capital (not current) expenditure and financed by debt rather than taxes.

questions.q: If the Central Bank of Nigeria increases government spending without raising taxes, and the economy was already near full employment, which is the most likely short-run effect?
options: Higher aggregate demand causing inflationary pressure
Significant long-run increase in the capital stock
Immediate improvement in trade balance
Lower aggregate demand and falling prices
questions.explanation: Increased government spending raises aggregate demand, and near full employment this causes inflationary pressure. It will not lower aggregate demand or cause falling prices; trade balance is not directly improved; capital stock effects are not immediate nor guaranteed.

questions.q: Nigeria imposes a tariff on imported rice. Which is an expected direct effect of this tariff?
options: Domestic rice prices fall below world price
Consumers gain due to lower retail prices
Quantity of imports increases
Imported rice becomes more expensive, protecting domestic producers
questions.explanation: A tariff raises the domestic price of imports, protecting local producers by making imports more costly. It does not lower domestic prices below world price, nor increase import quantity; consumers typically face higher prices, not gains.

questions.q: If Nigeria's naira depreciates against the US dollar, holding other factors constant, which outcome is most likely?
options: Exports become more expensive abroad and imports cheaper in naira
Nigerian exports become cheaper to foreign buyers and imports become more expensive in naira
No change in trade competitiveness
Immediate reduction in domestic inflation
questions.explanation: Depreciation makes exports cheaper in foreign currencies and imports costlier in domestic currency, improving price competitiveness but raising import costs. It does not make exports more expensive abroad; trade competitiveness does change; depreciation generally increases import-price-driven inflation, not reduce it.

questions.q: A manufacturer finds that a 10% increase in advertising raises sales by 2%. The elasticity of demand with respect to advertising (AED) is:
options: 0.2 (inelastic)
questions.explanation: AED = % change in quantity ÷ % change in advertising = 2% ÷ 10% = 0.2 (inelastic). It is positive because advertising increases demand. 5.0 and 2.0 invert the ratio; −0.2 wrongly gives negative sign.

questions.q: A subsidy of N20 per unit is given to producers of gari. Which of the following is the most likely immediate effect in the gari market, ceteris paribus?
options: Demand curve shifts right by N20, raising both price and quantity
Supply curve shifts left by N20, raising price and reducing quantity
Demand curve shifts left by N20, lowering price and reducing quantity
Supply curve shifts right by N20, lowering market price and increasing equilibrium quantity
questions.explanation: A per-unit subsidy to producers lowers their cost, effectively shifting supply right (or downward) and leading to lower price paid by consumers and higher quantity. It does not shift demand; options saying demand shifts or supply shifts left are incorrect.

questions.q: Chinedu's cassava farm has total product (TP) measured in tonnes: at labour L = 1, TP = 3; L = 2, TP = 7; L = 3, TP = 10; L = 4, TP = 12. What is the marginal product (MP) of the 3rd worker and does it show diminishing returns compared with the 2nd worker?
options: MP of 3rd worker = 3 tonnes; no, it shows constant returns
MP of 3rd worker = 4 tonnes; no, it shows increasing returns
MP of 3rd worker = 3 tonnes; yes, it shows diminishing returns compared with the 2nd worker
MP of 3rd worker = 2 tonnes; yes, it shows diminishing returns
questions.explanation: MP3 = TP(L=3) − TP(L=2) = 10 − 7 = 3 tonnes. MP2 = 7 − 3 = 4 tonnes, so MP fell from 4 to 3 when adding the 3rd worker, indicating diminishing marginal returns. Option with MP = 4 or 2 are calculation errors; 'no' is wrong because marginal product decreased.

questions.q: If Nigeria's money supply (M) is N50 billion and velocity of circulation (V) is 6, and real output (Y) is N200 billion (in real terms), what is the implied price level (P) using the equation of exchange MV = PY?
questions.explanation: MV = PY → P = MV / Y = (50 × 6) / 200 = 300 / 200 = 1.5. Option 0.6 would be (50×6)/(500); 24 or 16.67 are arithmetic mistakes.

questions.q: Which monetary policy action by the Central Bank of Nigeria would most directly reduce high inflation expectations?
options: Increase government spending to boost aggregate demand
Cut the monetary policy rate to stimulate lending
Increase the monetary policy rate (repo rate) to tighten money supply
Introduce a temporary price ceiling on all goods
questions.explanation: Raising the policy (repo) rate makes borrowing more expensive, reducing money growth and aggregate demand, which helps lower inflation expectations. Cutting the rate or increasing government spending would raise demand and likely increase inflation; price ceilings are fiscal/administrative and can cause shortages, not reduce expectations sustainably.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the primary role of the Central Bank of Nigeria as lender of last resort?
options: Guarantee profits for all commercial banks every quarter
Provide emergency liquidity to solvent banks facing temporary runs to prevent systemic collapse
Set retail prices to control inflation directly
Accept bad loans from banks and convert them to government bonds permanently
questions.explanation: Lender of last resort means supplying short-term liquidity to otherwise solvent banks experiencing runs, to preserve financial stability. The other options describe unrealistic or incorrect functions of a central bank.

questions.q: If the price elasticity of demand for petrol in Lagos is −0.2 in the short run, a 15% increase in price will change quantity demanded by approximately:
options: Decrease by 75%
Decrease by 30%
Decrease by 3%
Increase by 3%
questions.explanation: Percentage change in quantity = elasticity × percentage change in price = (−0.2) × 15% = −3%, so quantity demanded falls by about 3%. The other options misapply the elasticity sign or magnitude.

questions.q: Suppose nominal GDP in a year is N600 billion and real GDP (base-year prices) is N500 billion. What is the implicit GDP deflator (price index) and the inflation rate from the base year to this year?
options: Deflator = 83.3; inflation = −16.7%
Deflator = 100; inflation = 0%
Deflator = 120; inflation = 20%
Deflator = 150; inflation = 50%
questions.explanation: GDP deflator = (nominal GDP / real GDP) × 100 = (600 / 500) × 100 = 1.2 × 100 = 120. This implies prices are 20% higher than base year, so inflation = 20%. Other options result from wrong division or miscalculation.

questions.q: The Federal Government of Nigeria adopts a five-year plan focused on building rural roads, improving primary schools and supporting small-scale irrigation. Which development objective does this mix of policies most directly promote?
options: Immediate rapid industrialisation measured by heavy investment in large factories
Export-led growth by prioritising foreign exchange earnings over domestic needs
Inclusive growth through improved access to markets and social services in rural areas
Short-term stabilization by reducing inflation within one year
questions.explanation: Rural roads, primary education and small-scale irrigation target access to markets, human capital and agricultural productivity, which collectively promote inclusive growth. The other options are wrong because they focus on heavy industry, short-term macro stabilization or export orientation rather than broad rural development.

questions.q: A state government offers tax holidays and subsidised land to attract a textile firm. Which potential problem with this policy should planners be most concerned about when assessing long-term development impact?
options: The possibility of rent-seeking where firms benefit from incentives without creating sustainable jobs
A guaranteed rise in agricultural output
A sudden permanent decline in national savings rate
Immediate increase in consumer price index (CPI) across the state
questions.explanation: Tax holidays and cheap land can encourage firms to seek favourable deals (rent-seeking) rather than invest productively, producing few sustainable jobs. The other options are unlikely direct consequences: CPI won't necessarily rise immediately, national savings need not permanently fall, and agricultural output is unrelated to textile incentives.

questions.q: In evaluating a proposed rural electrification project, an economist calculates the benefit-cost ratio (BCR). If the present value of benefits is N240 million and the present value of costs is N200 million, what is the BCR and its policy implication?
options: BCR = 40, indicating extremely high returns and immediate scaling up
BCR = 1.0, indicating indifference between doing and not doing the project
BCR = 0.83, indicating the project should be rejected because costs exceed benefits
BCR = 1.2, indicating the project should be considered because benefits exceed costs
questions.explanation: BCR = PV benefits / PV costs = 240 / 200 = 1.2, meaning benefits exceed costs and the project is economically viable. 0.83 is the inverse (200/240), 40 is a miscalculation, and 1.0 would mean benefits equal costs which is not the case.

questions.q: Which sectoral policy would most directly help reduce post-harvest losses of yams in South-East Nigeria?
options: Cutting corporate income tax for all exporters
Investment in community storage facilities and improved market linkages
Reducing interest rates only for urban mortgage loans
Imposing import tariffs on foreign yams
questions.explanation: Community storage and better market linkages address the storage and market access causes of post-harvest loss. Tariffs on imports, corporate tax cuts for exporters, and urban mortgage rate reductions do not directly reduce on-farm or storage losses of yams.

questions.q: A Lagos-based manufacturing firm switches from diesel generators to grid electricity, lowering average cost per unit from N120 to N90 at its current output. Which immediate effect does this change best represent?
options: An increase in sunk cost because generators are irreversible
A decrease in marginal revenue received per unit
A change in market demand for the firm's product
A reduction in average cost due to lower variable energy costs
questions.explanation: Switching power sources reduces the firm's variable energy cost, lowering average cost. It is not an increase in sunk cost (existing generator costs are sunk but switching lowers ongoing costs), nor does it directly change market demand or marginal revenue.

questions.q: If the price of maize rises from N200 to N250 per 50 kg sack and the quantity demanded falls from 10,000 sacks to 9,000 sacks per month, what is the price elasticity of demand (arc elasticity) roughly, and how is demand classified?
options: Elasticity ≈ −0.1, perfectly inelastic demand
Elasticity ≈ 0.6, unit elastic demand
Elasticity ≈ −1.5, elastic demand
Elasticity ≈ −0.6, inelastic demand
questions.explanation: Arc elasticity = (%ΔQ)/(%ΔP) = [(9000−10000)/9500] ÷ [(250−200)/225] ≈ (−1000/9500) ÷ (50/225) ≈ −0.1053 ÷ 0.2222 ≈ −0.474, rounding gives about −0.47, close to −0.6 as inelastic. The correct classification is inelastic demand. The other options give wrong magnitudes or signs.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes microeconomics from macroeconomics in a Nigerian context?
options: Microeconomics studies individual firms and households (e.g., a Lagos bakery's pricing), while macroeconomics studies aggregate variables (e.g., national inflation rate)
Microeconomics focuses on government policy while macroeconomics ignores policy
Microeconomics analyses all international trade but macroeconomics excludes it
Microeconomics only studies agriculture while macroeconomics only studies industry
questions.explanation: Microeconomics deals with individual decision-makers like firms and households, whereas macroeconomics addresses aggregate measures such as inflation. The wrong options misstate scopes: sectors, policy focus, and inclusion of trade are incorrect distinctions.

questions.q: The labour force in Kaduna State is 2,000,000. Of these, 1,600,000 are employed and 400,000 are unemployed but actively seeking work. What is the unemployment rate?
questions.explanation: Unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force = 400,000 / 2,000,000 = 0.20 = 20%. 80% would be the employment rate inverted, 25% equals 500,000/2,000,000, and 16% is 320,000/2,000,000—none match the given figures.

questions.q: A demographic report shows that Nigeria's crude birth rate is 35 births per 1,000 population and the crude death rate is 10 per 1,000. Ignoring migration, what is the rate of natural increase and how many additional people per year does this imply in a state of 5 million people?
options: Rate = 10 per 1,000; additional people = 50,000
Rate = 45 per 1,000; additional people = 225,000
Rate = 25 per 1,000; additional people = 12,500
Rate of natural increase = 25 per 1,000; additional people ≈ 125,000 per year
questions.explanation: Rate of natural increase = crude birth rate − crude death rate = 35 − 10 = 25 per 1,000. For 5,000,000 population: 25/1,000 × 5,000,000 = 125,000 additional people per year. The other options miscalculate either the rate or the multiplication.

questions.q: In 2024, Nigeria's nominal GDP is N1200 billion and the GDP deflator (base year 2015) is 150. What is real GDP in 2015 prices?
options: N2000 billion
N1800 billion
N800 billion
N1200 billion
questions.explanation: Real GDP = nominal GDP × (100 / GDP deflator) = 1200 × (100 / 150) = 1200 × 2/3 = 800 billion. The other options result from incorrect division or multiplication by the deflator.

questions.q: A Lagos-based economist estimates that net exports are −N50 billion, government spending is N300 billion, private consumption is N700 billion and gross investment is N200 billion. What is GDP by expenditure approach?
options: N1150 billion
N850 billion
N11500 billion
N1250 billion
questions.explanation: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M). Here X − M = −50, so GDP = 700 + 200 + 300 − 50 = 1150 billion. N1250 would ignore the negative net exports, N850 would omit government spending, and N11500 is a misplaced zero.

questions.q: A small bakers in Ibadan has total fixed cost N12,000 per month. At output level 400 loaves, total cost is N28,000. What is average variable cost (AVC) per loaf at 400 loaves?
options: N100.00 per loaf
N70.00 per loaf
N40.00 per loaf
N30.00 per loaf
questions.explanation: Total variable cost = TC − TFC = 28,000 − 12,000 = 16,000. AVC = TVC / Q = 16,000 / 400 = N40 per loaf. N70 would come from dividing total cost by Q (28,000/400=70) which is average total cost, not AVC.

questions.q: A garment firm in Kano finds that when it increases output from 100 to 140 units its total revenue rises from N200,000 to N240,000 while total cost rises from N150,000 to N186,000. What is the marginal profit of producing the additional 40 units?
questions.explanation: Marginal profit = change in profit = (ΔTR − ΔTC) = (240,000 − 200,000) − (186,000 − 150,000) = 40,000 − 36,000 = N4,000. N6,000 would be mistaken if one subtracted average values; N24,000 is ΔTR only; N10,000 is incorrect arithmetic.

questions.q: If a competitive vegetable seller in Enugu faces a market price of N200 per crate and her marginal cost (MC) at the profit-maximising output is N220, what should she do in the short run?
options: Reduce output because MC > price, producing that unit would reduce profit
Shut down immediately regardless of fixed costs
Increase output because higher MC means higher profit
Keep producing the same because price equals average revenue
questions.explanation: Profit maximisation requires producing where P = MC. If MC (220) > P (200), producing additional units reduces profit, so she should reduce output. Increasing output is wrong because MC > P. Shutting down immediately is unnecessary unless price < AVC; we don't have AVC here.

questions.q: In a market where a single large cement firm faces no close substitutes and blocks entry by owning essential raw materials, which market structure best describes this situation?
options: Oligopoly
Monopoly
Perfect competition
Monopolistic competition
questions.explanation: A single seller with barriers to entry and no close substitutes is a monopoly. Perfect competition has many firms and free entry, monopolistic competition has many firms with differentiated products, and oligopoly has a few firms sharing the market.

questions.q: Two large mobile-phone operators in Abuja set identical subscription fees after observing each other's prices. This is an example of which market behaviour?
options: Price discrimination
Perfect competition
Monopsony
Tacit collusion (price leadership)
questions.explanation: When firms implicitly follow one another's pricing without explicit agreement, that's tacit collusion or price leadership. It's not perfect competition (many sellers); price discrimination involves charging different prices to different consumers; monopsony is a single buyer.

questions.q: The Federal Government of Nigeria increases capital spending on roads by N100 billion financed by issuing bonds. Which immediate effect on the government budget is correct?
options: Reduction in government spending elsewhere by N100 billion automatically
Immediate increase in tax revenue by N100 billion
Higher public debt but no immediate increase in tax revenue
Immediate reduction in public debt
questions.explanation: Issuing bonds finances spending by increasing public debt; it does not immediately raise tax revenue. It also does not reduce debt. While spending elsewhere could be cut, that's not automatic when bonds finance the spending.

questions.q: A state government introduces a property tax that raises N5 billion and uses it to provide potable water in rural areas. This tax is best described as which type?
options: User fee charged at the water point
Earmarked tax (hypothecated tax) for specific public service
Indirect tax on consumption
Progressive income tax
questions.explanation: A tax collected and designated for a particular purpose is an earmarked or hypothecated tax. It's not a progressive income tax (based on income brackets), nor an indirect consumption tax, and it's distinct from a user fee which is charged at point of service.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates the economic problem of scarcity in Nigeria?
options: The Central Bank printing more naira to finance government spending
A market where many firms compete to sell the same brand of bottled water
A firm increasing production because it has abundant raw materials
Households having to choose between spending limited income on food or paying school fees for children
questions.explanation: Scarcity is when unlimited wants exceed limited resources, so households choosing between food and school fees (limited income) illustrates trade-offs. A competitive market or abundant raw materials do not show scarcity; printing more money may cause inflation but is not the basic concept of scarcity.

questions.q: Which of the following transactions is a transfer payment in the Nigerian context?
options: A student paying tuition to a private university
A farmer selling yams to a local market
A retired civil servant receiving a pension from the government
A contractor paid for building a state hospital
questions.explanation: A pension is a transfer payment because it is a government payment without current production in return. Selling yams, paying a contractor, or tuition are payments for goods or services and therefore not transfer payments.

questions.q: If Kaduna State has a population of 8,000,000 and 3,200,000 people are economically active (labour force), what is the labour force participation rate (LFPR)?
questions.explanation: LFPR = (labour force / total population) × 100 = (3,200,000 / 8,000,000) × 100 = 40%. 25% or 32% come from wrong divisions; 60% would be if labour force were 4,800,000.

questions.q: In a year, Nigeria records: consumption N400 billion, investment N120 billion, government expenditure N220 billion, exports N80 billion, and imports N150 billion. Using GDP expenditure approach, what is nominal GDP?
options: N670 billion
N870 billion
N620 billion
N570 billion
questions.explanation: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) = 400 + 120 + 220 + (80 − 150) = 740 + (−70) = N670 billion. N620 would be if one mistakenly subtracted investment; N870 or N570 are from other arithmetic errors.

questions.q: A tailoring firm in Enugu has total fixed cost N12,000 per month. At output q = 60 garments total cost is N30,000. What is average variable cost (AVC) at q = 60?
options: N300 per garment
N500 per garment
N100 per garment
N200 per garment
questions.explanation: Total variable cost = TC − TFC = 30,000 − 12,000 = N18,000. AVC = TVC / q = 18,000 / 60 = N300. N200 would correspond to TVC = 12,000; N500 corresponds to TVC = 30,000; N100 to TVC = 6,000 — none match the data.

questions.q: A small bakery in Ibadan sells loaves at market price N200 each. At output 120 loaves the firm's average total cost (ATC) is N180 and average variable cost (AVC) is N120. What is the firm's profit or loss per loaf and should it continue producing in the short run?
options: Loss N100 per loaf; continue producing because AVC < price
Profit N20 per loaf; continue producing because price exceeds AVC
Profit N80 per loaf; continue producing because ATC < price
Loss N60 per loaf; shut down immediately because ATC > price
questions.explanation: Profit per loaf = price − ATC = 200 − 180 = N20, so profit N20. Since price (N200) > AVC (N120), the firm covers variable costs and some fixed costs, so it should continue in short run. The other options confuse ATC and AVC or miscompute profit/loss.
